game.title: STEM IS FOR YOU
game.subtitle: A Girls Go STEM museum escape
intro: It's after closing time and you're locked inside the Museum of Science & Technology.
Someone has erased the names of brilliant women scientists from the exhibits.
Restore every name, collect the letters of each door code and find your way out!
game.finaleHint: Walk to the empty pedestal in front of the mirror.
game.finaleTagline: Every name in this room started as a curious girl. The 13th pedestal is waiting for you.

exhibits.name: Ada Lovelace
exhibits.context: In the 1840s, a young English mathematician studied the Analytical Engine, a giant mechanical calculating machine designed by her friend Charles Babbage. She translated an article about the machine and added her own notes, three times longer than the article itself. In one note she wrote out, step by step, how the machine could calculate a special series of numbers.
exhibits.question: What did she write?
clues: In the 1840s, she wrote notes about a machine that was never fully built.
She imagined that machines could one day create music, not just numbers.
Her notes give a machine step-by-step instructions to calculate numbers.
exhibits.reveal: Ada Lovelace (1815–1852) wrote the first algorithm for Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine. Fun fact: her father was the poet Lord Byron, and the programming language "Ada" is named after her.

exhibits.name: Marie Curie
exhibits.achievement: Nobel Prizes in Physics and Chemistry
exhibits.context: This Polish-French scientist studied mysterious, invisible rays coming from a dark mineral called pitchblende. Working with her husband Pierre in a cold shed, she found that the rays came from elements nobody had ever seen before. She named the first one after the country where she was born, which at that time was not even on the map.
exhibits.question: Which element did she name after her homeland?
clues: She discovered two new elements.
More than 100 years later, her notebooks are still radioactive.
Her homeland was Poland.
exhibits.reveal: Marie Curie (1867–1934) discovered polonium and radium and is the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences (Physics and Chemistry). Fun fact: to read her notebooks today, you must wear protective clothing.

exhibits.name: Mileva Marić
exhibits.context: She grew up in Serbia and was one of the first women to study physics and mathematics at the Polytechnic in Zurich, Switzerland. There she met a fellow student who later became one of the most famous scientists in history. They studied together, shared their love of physics, married in 1903 and had three children.
exhibits.question: Who was her husband?
clues: In 1896, she was the only woman in her class at the Zurich Polytechnic.
She studied the same subject as her husband and discussed his early ideas with him.
He became world-famous for E = mc².
exhibits.reveal: Mileva Marić (1875–1948) was a Serbian physicist from Titel. Historians still debate how much she contributed to Einstein's early work. Fun fact: under their divorce agreement, Einstein's Nobel Prize money went to her.

exhibits.name: Rosalind Franklin
exhibits.context: This British chemist was an expert in X-ray crystallography: shining X-rays through tiny structures and studying the patterns they leave on film. In 1952 her team took an extremely sharp X-ray picture of a long molecule found inside every living cell. The X-shaped pattern in that picture showed how the molecule is built.
exhibits.question: What did Photo 51 show?
clues: Her most famous X-ray image is called "Photo 51".
The image revealed a twisted, spiral shape: a double helix.
That shape is in every cell of your body and carries your genes.
exhibits.reveal: Rosalind Franklin (1920–1958) captured the image that revealed the structure of DNA. Others used her data without her knowledge, and the Nobel Prize went to three men.

exhibits.name: Lise Meitner
exhibits.context: This Austrian physicist spent her life studying the nucleus, the tiny centre of an atom. In 1938 her colleagues shot neutrons at uranium atoms and got a strange result they could not explain. She worked out that the uranium nucleus had split into two smaller pieces, releasing an enormous amount of energy.
exhibits.question: What did she explain?
clues: Element 109, meitnerium, is named after her.
On a snowy walk in 1938, she worked out why an atom had split.
The same process powers nuclear power plants today.
exhibits.reveal: Lise Meitner (1878–1968) explained nuclear fission, but the Nobel Prize went only to her colleague Otto Hahn. Fun fact: she refused to work on the atomic bomb.

exhibits.name: Hedy Lamarr
exhibits.context: She was a famous Hollywood film star in the 1930s and 1940s, but in her free time she loved to invent things. With a composer friend she patented a "secret communication system" in which the radio signal jumps quickly between many frequencies, so nobody can block it or listen in. Today the same idea helps your wireless devices share the airwaves without getting in each other's way.
exhibits.question: Which everyday technology uses her idea?
clues: In World War II, she invented a way to stop enemies from jamming radio-controlled torpedoes.
Her idea: a signal that keeps "hopping" between frequencies, like fingers on piano keys.
You probably used her idea today, to connect your phone without a cable.
exhibits.reveal: Hedy Lamarr (1914–2000) was a Hollywood star by day and an inventor by night. Her frequency-hopping invention was only recognised in 1997.

exhibits.name: Katherine Johnson
exhibits.context: She was an African-American mathematician who worked at NASA when complex calculations were still done by people, who were called "computers". She worked out exactly which path a spacecraft must fly, and where it would come back down to Earth. Without her precise numbers, astronauts could not have travelled safely into orbit and to the Moon.
exhibits.question: What was her superpower at NASA?
clues: An astronaut refused to fly until she personally checked the computer's numbers.
She calculated the paths of spacecraft by hand.
Her story is told in the film "Hidden Figures".
exhibits.reveal: Katherine Johnson (1918–2020), a NASA mathematician, calculated flight paths for the first American in orbit and for Apollo 11.

exhibits.name: Valentina Tereshkova
exhibits.context: She was a textile-factory worker who loved parachute jumping, and she was chosen from more than 400 applicants for a very special mission. In June 1963 she flew the Vostok 6 spacecraft for almost three days, all by herself. At the end of the flight she ejected from her capsule and landed safely with a parachute.
exhibits.question: Where was she the first woman to go?
clues: Before her big mission, she worked in a textile factory and loved parachute jumping.
Her call sign was "Chaika", which means "Seagull".
She was the first woman to see the whole planet from above.
exhibits.reveal: Valentina Tereshkova (born 1937) became the first woman in space in 1963, orbiting Earth 48 times. Fun fact: she is still the only woman who has flown a space mission completely alone.

exhibits.name: Margaret Hamilton
exhibits.context: She was a computer scientist at MIT who led the team writing the software for NASA's Apollo spacecraft. Her programs could notice when the onboard computer had too much to do and keep working on only the most important jobs. Minutes before a world-famous landing, alarms went off, and her software kept the astronauts safe.
exhibits.question: Which mission did her code save?
clues: Her 4-year-old daughter, playing with a simulator, helped her find a dangerous bug.
A famous photo shows her next to a stack of printed code as tall as she is.
Thanks to her code, humans walked on the Moon in 1969.
exhibits.reveal: Margaret Hamilton (born 1936) led the team that wrote Apollo's flight software. She invented the term "software engineering".

exhibits.name: Stephanie Kwolek
exhibits.context: This American chemist worked at the DuPont company, looking for a strong, lightweight fibre to make car tyres. One experiment produced a thin, cloudy liquid that looked like a failure. When it was spun into threads, it turned out to be incredibly strong and heat-resistant.
exhibits.question: What did she invent?
clues: In 1965 she found a strange, cloudy liquid that colleagues wanted to throw away.
She spun it into a fibre five times stronger than steel, for its weight.
Police officers and firefighters wear it in protective vests and helmets.
exhibits.reveal: Stephanie Kwolek (1923–2014) invented Kevlar. Fun fact: she took a chemistry job to save money for medical school, and then never left.

exhibits.name: Jennifer Doudna & Emmanuelle Charpentier
exhibits.context: These two scientists, one American and one French, studied the clever way bacteria remember and destroy the viruses that attack them. Together they turned that natural defence into a simple tool that can find one exact spot in DNA and cut it. Scientists now use it to study diseases, develop new medicines and grow better crops.
exhibits.question: Which field of science?
clues: They studied how bacteria defend themselves against viruses.
They turned that defence into a tool that can cut DNA exactly where you want.
Their tool is called CRISPR, the "genetic scissors".
exhibits.reveal: Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, the first science Nobel shared only by women.

exhibits.name: Maryam Mirzakhani
exhibits.achievement: First woman to win the Fields Medal
exhibits.context: She was an Iranian mathematician who became a professor at Stanford University in the USA. She studied curved surfaces, shapes like doughnuts and pretzels with many holes, and the paths that run across them. In 2014 she received the most famous award in mathematics, which is given only once every four years.
exhibits.question: Which prize was she the first woman to win?
clues: As a girl in Tehran, she dreamed of becoming a writer.
She drew huge doodles on paper spread across her floor to study curved surfaces.
It is often called the "Nobel Prize of mathematics".
exhibits.reveal: Maryam Mirzakhani (1977–2017) studied the geometry of curved surfaces and became the first woman to win the Fields Medal in 2014.
